idiom_name: DispatchQueue (serial or concurrent) or OperationQueue as dispatcher+pools; TaskGroup for structured concurrency
implementation_notes: Dispatch is the dispatcher in the literal sense: a DispatchQueue is a FIFO queue of work items executed serially or concurrently on a system-managed thread pool, so a serial queue is a single ordered performer, a global concurrent queue (or DispatchQueue(attributes: .concurrent)) is a performer pool, and DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform is the data-parallel form. OperationQueue layers maxConcurrentOperationCount, dependencies and cancellation on top, which is how the degree of parallelism is bounded. From Swift 5.5 the structured-concurrency form is withTaskGroup: the group is the performer pool, addTask() is the dispatch step, priority and task-local values are inherited, and the group always waits for its children. Choose GCD when you need queue-level control or QoS; choose a task group when the rest of the code is async/await.
pitfalls: DispatchQueue.sync onto the main queue deadlocks (documented): the dispatcher must never synchronously hand work back to the queue it is running on.

A blocked task on a concurrent queue makes the system create additional threads and can exhaust them (documented 'avoiding excessive thread creation'); blocking belongs on dedicated queues, not the global pool.
Cancellation is cooperative in both models: Operation.cancel() and TaskGroup.cancelAll() only set a flag, so long-running performers must check it.
A TaskGroup always waits for all children before returning, even if the body returns early; cancelAll() is the only way to shorten that wait, and it still runs the children's cleanup.
Async closures capture self strongly and outlive the call that scheduled them; long-lived dispatchers leak objects unless captures are weak or explicitly released.
